home.intro: A channel rack, a piano roll, a playlist and a mixer, with one signal path from an oscillator through its effect chain to a mixer insert and out the master.
home.workflowBody: There are no floating windows, no layouts to arrange and no plugin scan at startup, so a session opens where the last one ended.
home.predictableBody: Channel rack, piano roll, playlist, mixer and score, always in that order, beside one instrument panel. A channel row carries its own volume, pan and on/off switch; a mixer strip carries its own effect chain.
home.signalBody: Three oscillators into an amp envelope, into the channel’s effect chain, into a mixer insert, into the master. Every knob on that path is automatable from its own right-click menu.
home.completeBody: Ten effects, forty factory presets, wavetables, an FM matrix, SoundFont playback and a renderer. Two dependencies in the whole build, and no plugin format to scan.
home.openBody: Every line is on GitHub under the AGPLv3, this site included. Free to use for any purpose, with no warranty of any kind.

mcp.title: Control dew from an agent
mcp.lead: dew runs a Model Context Protocol server inside the application, so a coding agent can read and change the project you have open.
mcp.howBody: Turn it on under Audio → MCP. dew listens on the loopback interface only. The first time a client connects, dew asks whether to allow it, and whether it may only read or change things too. Every change it makes is one step of your undo history.
mcp.connectBody: The MCP settings panel shows the address and the exact command. The port is not fixed, so copy the command rather than typing it.
mcp.surfaceBody: One address space covers every value in the document. Five fields — target, id, group, slot and param — name any parameter of any oscillator, envelope, sample, soundfont, effect, mixer insert or the master, and the same five say what an automation curve is pointed at.
mcp.scoreBody: For anything longer than a few bars, an agent writes dew’s arrangement language and compiles it, which takes one call rather than one per note.

score.title: The score language
score.lead: A text description of a whole piece, compiled into patterns, notes and playlist clips.
score.whatBody: Sketching a whole arrangement faster than you can draw it. You write a key, a metre, a harmonic progression, rhythms, voicings and melody shapes; the compiler works out the notes. It is the fifth tab, checked as you type and compiled with ⌘R. The text is stored in the project, so recompiling updates what it wrote last time and leaves anything you have since edited by hand alone.
score.noExpressions: There is no expression language: no arithmetic, no variables, no conditionals. Every value is a literal, so completion is a table lookup and the compiler reads the step grid off the durations the text names before it generates anything.
score.limitsBody: dew stores one tempo and one metre for a whole project, so a section in 3/4 inside a 4/4 project is not expressible. A note’s position is a whole number of steps, so the grid is the least common multiple of what the durations need: sixteenths and eighth-note triplets meet at twelve. The grid stops at sixteen steps to a beat, so a thirty-second alongside any triplet would need twenty-four, and the compiler refuses it and names the two durations that collide.

setup.title: Setup
setup.lead: dew builds from source on macOS, Windows and Linux. Two CMake commands on each, once that platform’s tools are installed.
setup.presetsBody: release is the one to build for normal use. The first configure fetches JUCE and Catch2 from source and caches them per machine under `~/.cache/CPM`; every configure after that reads the cache.
setup.checkBody: One command, and it runs what CI runs: the dependency pins, the formatting, a warnings-as-errors build, the tests, and a check that every generated file matches what produces it.

site.mp3Note: MP3 export needs lame installed separately: the option stays greyed out until lame is on your PATH. WAV, FLAC and MIDI need nothing.

download.title: Download
download.lead: Builds of dew for macOS, Windows and Linux, from the latest release. It is a working prototype.
download.getBody: Every link points at the latest release. Older versions stay on the releases page.
download.firstRunTitle: The first time you run it
download.firstRunBody: None of these builds is signed, so macOS and Windows each block the first launch.
download.verifyBody: Every release carries SHA256SUMS.txt, and every asset is covered by a Sigstore build attestation. The attestation records the repository, the workflow and the commit the file was built from.
download.buildBody: Two CMake commands on any of the three. A binary you build yourself is not blocked on first launch.
